title: USB Keystrokes
html:
USB Keystrokes

If you have a pcap containing the communication via USB of a keyboard like the following one:

For a keyboard using the HID boot protocol, each Interrupt IN report has a fixed 8-byte layout: one modifier byte, one reserved byte, and six keycode bytes. The host compares successive reports and maps keycodes to HID usages to reconstruct key events.[8]

For general capture triage, see Pcap Inspection.

USB HID report basics

The standard boot keyboard input report is structured as follows.[8][9]

Byte Meaning
0 Modifier bitmap (0x02 = Left Shift, 0x20 = Right Shift, 0x40 = Right Alt, etc.). Multiple bits can be set simultaneously.
1 Reserved byte; unused reports should normally set it to zero. OEM or system-specific use is not portable.
2-7 Up to six concurrent keycodes in USB usage ID format (0x04 = a, 0x1E = 1). 0x00 means "no key".

In the boot layout, usage ID 0x01 (Keyboard ErrorRollOver) is reported in all key slots when more than six non-modifier keys are pressed; it can also signal an unrecognizable combination.[8][9] Understanding this layout helps when you only have the raw usb.capdata bytes.

Extracting HID data from a PCAP

Identify the keyboard interface first

On busy captures, identify the HID keyboard before dumping any reports. A reliable starting point is the interface descriptor response:[3][8]

usb.transfer_type == 0x02 && usb.endpoint_address.direction == 1 && usb.bDescriptorType == 4 && usb.bInterfaceClass == 3

The HID class defines these interface values:[8]

  • subclass == 1 is the Boot Interface Subclass; with protocol == 1 it identifies a boot keyboard
  • protocol == 2 identifies a boot mouse
  • protocol == 0 means no boot protocol; inspect the HID report descriptor instead of assuming an 8-byte layout

A boot-capable interface is not proof that boot protocol is active. HID devices initialize in report protocol. The host selects boot mode with SET_PROTOCOL (bRequest = 0x0b, wValue = 0); wValue = 1 selects report protocol. If enumeration is in the capture, check the request for the keyboard interface (wIndex) before using an eight-byte boot decoder. If it is absent, verify the observed report layout instead of inferring the mode from the interface descriptor.[8][10]

tshark -r usb.pcapng -Y 'usb.setup.bRequest == 0x0b' -T fields \
  -e frame.number -e usb.bus_id -e usb.device_address \
  -e usb.setup.wIndex -e usb.setup.wValue

Once the interface is known, pin your filters to usb.bus_id, usb.device_address, and if possible usb.bInterfaceNumber before exporting anything.

Wireshark workflow

  1. Isolate the device: filter on interrupt IN traffic from the keyboard, e.g. usb.transfer_type == 0x01 && usb.endpoint_address.direction == 1 && usb.device_address == 3.
  2. Add useful columns: right-click the Leftover Capture Data field (usb.capdata) and your preferred usbhid.* fields (e.g. usbhid.boot_report.keyboard.keycode_1) to follow keystrokes without opening every frame.[11]
  3. Hide empty reports: apply !(usb.capdata == 00:00:00:00:00:00:00:00) to drop idle frames.
  4. Export for post-processing: File -> Export Packet Dissections -> As CSV, include frame.number, usb.src, usb.capdata, and decoded modifier fields such as usbhid.boot_report.keyboard.modifier.left_shift and usbhid.boot_report.keyboard.modifier.right_alt to script the reconstruction later.[10][11]

Command-line workflow

The classic extraction pattern—dump usb.capdata, drop idle reports, and map usage IDs—appears in the original 2017 analysis and its walkthrough.[1][2]

The ctf-usb-keyboard-parser repository automates the classic tshark + sed pipeline:[5]

tshark -r ./usb.pcap -Y 'usb.capdata && usb.data_len == 8' -T fields -e usb.capdata | sed 's/../:&/g2' > keystrokes.txt
python3 usbkeyboard.py ./keystrokes.txt

On newer captures, prefer Wireshark's decoded usbhid.data field and fall back to usb.capdata; write one payload per report to a per-device file:[7][10][11]

tshark -r usb.pcapng -Y "usb.capdata || usbhid.data" -T fields -E separator=$'\t' -e usb.src -e usb.capdata -e usbhid.data | \
  awk -F '\t' '{ payload = ($3 != "" ? $3 : $2); if (payload != "") print payload > "usbdata-" $1 ".txt" }'

Those per-device files can be fed to a decoder after normalizing the hex format it expects. If the capture came from BLE keyboards tunneled over GATT, filter on btatt.value && frame.len == 20 and dump the hex payloads before decoding.[7]

When the report is not the classic 8-byte boot report

A non-boot interface or a report ID can change the payload layout, so do not assume every keyboard report matches modifier,reserved,key1..key6.[8][11]

  • Prefer usbhid.data over usb.capdata when Wireshark has already parsed the HID layer.
  • If every line starts with a constant prefix or report ID, strip it with an offset-aware decoder rather than assuming byte 0 is always the modifier.[7]
  • Some USBPcap exports omit the reserved byte, so decoders that support --no-reserved or a custom offset save time.[7]
  • If the HID report descriptor or BLE HOGP report map is present in the capture, use it to recover the actual field layout before writing a parser.

Decode a report-protocol key bitmap

For a keyboard whose input report is a bitmap rather than six boot key slots, locate its HID report descriptor in the enumeration traffic. This filter finds frames where Wireshark decoded a Report Size item; open one and inspect the full descriptor. Start a new capture before plugging in the keyboard if the descriptor is missing.[11][12][13]

tshark -r usb.pcapng -Y 'usbhid.item.global.report_size' -T fields \
  -e frame.number -e usb.bus_id -e usb.device_address

For each keyboard Input report, note its Report ID (if any), Usage Page (0x07 for keyboard keys), Usage Minimum/Maximum, Report Size, Report Count, and whether each Input item is Variable or Array. Count all preceding Input fields and constant padding to find the key field's bit offset; report fields need not be byte-aligned. A one-bit Variable field with consecutive keyboard usages is a key-state bitmap: bit 0 of that field maps to its first declared usage, bit 1 to the next, and so on. An Array instead contains values resolved through the descriptor's usage range, not one pressed key per bit. If a Report ID is declared, first select reports with that prefix and skip its byte when calculating field offsets. Compare held-usage sets between consecutive reports of the same interface and Report ID to emit only new presses.[8][12][13]

Automating the decoding

  • ctf-usb-keyboard-parser remains handy for quick CTF challenges and already ships in the repository.[5]
  • CTF-Usb_Keyboard_Parser (main.py) parses both pcap and pcapng files natively, understands LinkTypeUsbLinuxMmapped/LinkTypeUsbPcap, and does not require tshark or another external dependency, so it is suitable for isolated sandboxes.[6]
  • USB-HID-decoders adds keyboard, mouse, and tablet visualizers. You can either run the extract_hid_data.sh helper (tshark backend) or extract_hid_data.py (scapy backend) and then feed the resulting text file to the decoder or replay modules to watch the keystrokes unfold.[7]

Stateful decoding matters

USB boot keyboards send reports at the idle rate even when there is no new key event, so captures may contain repeated reports before the release event. A practical decoder should:[3][8]

  • emit only newly pressed keycodes compared to the previous report
  • keep modifier state (Shift, Ctrl, AltGr) from byte 0 or parsed fields such as usbhid.boot_report.keyboard.modifier.left_shift and usbhid.boot_report.keyboard.modifier.right_alt
  • track toggle keys such as Caps Lock, because uppercase output is not controlled by Shift alone
  • remember that HID usage IDs are layout-agnostic: 0x1d is the physical z/y key position depending on the host keyboard layout.[9]

Quick Python decoder

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
NORMAL = {0x04:'a',0x05:'b',0x06:'c',0x07:'d',0x08:'e',0x09:'f',0x0a:'g',0x1c:'y',0x1d:'z',0x28:'\n',0x2d:'-',0x2e:'=',0x2f:'[',0x30:']',0x33:';',0x34:"'",0x36:',',0x37:'.'}
SHIFTED = {0x2d:'_',0x2e:'+',0x2f:'{',0x30:'}',0x33:':',0x34:'"',0x36:'<',0x37:'>'}
prev = set()
caps = False
for raw in sys.stdin:
    raw = raw.strip().replace(':', '')
    if len(raw) != 16:
        continue
    modifier = int(raw[0:2], 16)
    keycodes = [int(raw[i:i+2], 16) for i in range(4, 16, 2)]
    current = {k for k in keycodes if k}
    newly_pressed = [k for k in keycodes if k and k not in prev]
    shift = bool(modifier & 0x22)
    for keycode in newly_pressed:
        if keycode == 0x39:
            caps = not caps
            continue
        char = SHIFTED.get(keycode) if shift else None
        if char is None:
            char = NORMAL.get(keycode, '?')
            if char.isalpha() and (shift ^ caps):
                char = char.upper()
        sys.stdout.write(char)
    prev = current

Feed it with the plain hex lines dumped earlier to get an instant rough reconstruction without pulling a full parser into the environment. For non-US layouts this still reconstructs the physical key position, not necessarily the final glyph shown on the victim host.

Troubleshooting tips

  • If Wireshark does not populate usbhid.* fields, the HID report descriptor was probably not captured. Replug the keyboard while capturing or fall back to raw usb.capdata.
  • On Linux software captures, usbmon is the normal source; on Windows, Wireshark depends on the USBPcap extcap to see raw USB URBs at all.[4]
  • If the keyboard was attached through a hub or dock, confirm the interface descriptor first and then decode only that device/interface pair. Composite HID captures frequently mix keyboard and mouse reports.
  • Windows captures require the USBPcap extcap interface; make sure it survived Wireshark upgrades, as missing extcaps leave you with empty device lists.[4]
  • Always correlate the bus, device, and interface tuple (usb.bus_id, usb.device_address, usb.bInterfaceNumber; e.g. 1.9.1) before decoding anything — mixing multiple keyboards or storage devices leads to nonsense keystrokes.[10]
